data.body:
Most of us move through the world at a scroll's distance from it — saving places for later, accumulating images we never quite enter. I started going to the places that refused that transaction.

Photography, for me, is where light becomes language and landscape becomes something closer to a reckoning. The most honest photographs are not taken so much as they are waited for. Cold mornings, uncertain skies, the long stillness before the light does what you suspected it might. You raise the camera toward something you cannot yet fully see, and you commit to it anyway. That act of commitment — before the confirmation, before the histogram — is where the work actually lives.

An arch in sandstone, a gap in cloud, a corridor of trees at the edge of dark: these are not subjects. They are thresholds. The frame does not contain the view. It offers it, the way a window offers a room to the world beyond its walls. What interests me is not the destination on the other side but the moment of passage itself, that suspended instant when you are neither here nor there, when the landscape opens and asks something of you.

I have learned to stay in that moment rather than move through it. To treat the threshold as the thing itself.

data.line1: The land holds its breath before the shutter opens.
data.line2: We scroll past the image, save it for later, and move on. The daydream remains what it has always been: a beautiful moment we never quite arrive at.

data.body:
I started chasing the places that couldn’t be scrolled past.

The Infinite Arch is built on a belief that the most honest photographs aren’t taken — they’re waited for. They come to the photographer who arrives early, stays late, and returns when the light changes. Who understands that the arch in the rock and the arch of a life are describing the same passage: a threshold between what was and what’s possible.

I shoot with Fujifilm’s GFX medium format system because the format demands presence. You can’t spray and pray at 102 megapixels. You choose your moment, and you mean it. My kit is the GFX 100RF, the GFX 50R, the X-E5, and a Konica Hexar — each one chosen for what it sees, not what it proves.

This is photography as contemplation. Landscape as mirror. Light as metaphor.

Sean O’Connell didn’t say number 25 is technically perfect or compositionally superior. He said it was the quintessence of life. The difference matters to me. He was talking about the photograph that captured something true — not flawless, but undeniably alive. That’s the standard I’m chasing. Not the image that impresses, but the one that’s irreplaceable. The one I had to be cold for, had to wait for, had to raise the camera toward the impossible light and believe something was there before I could see it. This is what I came for. This is the quintessence of life.
data.closing: Welcome to the other side of the daydream.

portfolioWorks.description: Iceland. Guadalupe Peak. New Orleans. The locations accumulate not as destinations collected but as sites of patient attendance — places where the work of arriving gives way to the slower work of waiting. Waiting for light to shift across volcanic stone, for weather to break or deepen, for the particular moment that retroactively justifies every mile of the journey. Each expedition is a deliberate act of going somewhere in order to be still.
